                        "@type": "Answer",
                        "text": "cRPO (current Remaining Performance Obligations) is the 12-month forward-bookings figure on every public SaaS company's balance sheet. It is the dollar value of contracted revenue that will be recognized as revenue over the next 12 months. Required disclosure under FASB ASC 606 since 2018."
                  }
            },
            {
                  "@type": "Question",
                  "name": "How is cRPO different from ARR?",
                  "acceptedAnswer": {
                        "@type": "Answer",
                        "text": "cRPO comes from the balance sheet \u2014 audited, GAAP, and required by ASC 606 \u2014 and covers exactly the next 12 months of contracted revenue. ARR is management-disclosed (non-GAAP), is an annualized run-rate at a point in time, and its definition varies by company. cRPO is what the auditor signed off on; ARR is what management told you."
                  }
            },
            {
                  "@type": "Question",
                  "name": "Why does cRPO matter for SaaS diligence?",
                  "acceptedAnswer": {
                        "@type": "Answer",
                        "text": "cRPO is the leading indicator the trailing P&L cannot show. If cRPO grows faster than reported revenue, the forward book is compounding faster than recognition \u2014 bullish. If cRPO decelerates below revenue growth, the book is shrinking relative to recognition \u2014 bearish. It also survives auditor scrutiny in a way that management-defined ARR does not."
                  }
            },
            {
                  "@type": "Question",
                  "name": "What is the cRPO-RPO spread?",
                  "acceptedAnswer": {
                        "@type": "Answer",
                        "text": "The cRPO-RPO spread is the gap between 12-month cRPO growth and total RPO growth. A widening spread (cRPO growing faster than total RPO) means contract durations are shortening \u2014 customers are signing 2-year deals where they used to sign 3-year.   <h1>What is cRPO? The Operator's Guide to Current Remaining Performance Obligations</h1>
  <div class="post-meta">
    <span class="author">Pacer AI</span>
    <span>May 28, 2026</span>
  </div>
</div>

<!-- ═══════════════════════════════════════ CONTENT ═══════════════════════════════════════ -->
<div class="post-content">
<p><strong>cRPO — current Remaining Performance Obligations</strong> is the 12-month forward-bookings figure on every public SaaS company's balance sheet. It is the dollar value of contracted revenue that will be recognized over the next 12 months, audited under <a href="https://asc.fasb.org/topic&trid=49130388" target="_blank" rel="noopener">ASC 606</a>, and disclosed in every 10-Q and 10-K since 2018. For PE Operating Partners, CFOs, and M&A diligence teams, it is the cleanest leading indicator on SaaS performance. Cleaner than ARR, because ARR is whatever management says it is, and cRPO is what the auditor signed off on.</p>

<p>Most operators still treat ARR as the gold standard for forward revenue. That's a problem in 2026. Contract durations have been compressing across the industry, ARR definitions vary company-to-company, and three of the largest public SaaS companies (Workday, ServiceNow, and Atlassian) don't disclose ARR at all. If you anchor on ARR, you are flying blind on a meaningful share of the market.</p>

<h2>What is cRPO?</h2>

<p>cRPO stands for <strong>current Remaining Performance Obligations</strong>. It is the portion of total Remaining Performance Obligations (RPO) that the company expects to recognize as revenue within the next 12 months. Both metrics come from the same revenue footnote in the 10-Q and 10-K, required under <a href="https://www.fasb.org/page/PageContent?pageId=/standards/accounting-standards-codification.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">FASB ASC 606 — Revenue from Contracts with Customers</a>.</p>

<p>The mechanics are simple. When a SaaS company signs a multi-year contract, the full contract value sits on the balance sheet as a performance obligation. cRPO carves out the slice that will convert to revenue in the next four quarters. Total RPO captures everything beyond that — year two, year three, and any further-out commitments.</p>

<h2>How is cRPO different from ARR?</h2>

<p>The differences matter for diligence. ARR is a management-defined run-rate metric. cRPO is an auditable, GAAP-disclosed forward-bookings figure. They measure different things, and they are not interchangeable.</p>

<table>
  <thead>
    <tr><th></th><th>cRPO</th><th>ARR</th></tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><td><strong>Source</strong></td><td>Balance sheet (audited, GAAP)</td><td>Management-disclosed (non-GAAP)</td></tr>
    <tr><td><strong>Window</strong></td><td>Next 12 months only</td><td>Annualized run-rate at point in time</td></tr>
    <tr><td><strong>Includes</strong></td><td>Signed contracts, both billed and unbilled</td><td>Active recurring subscriptions at end of period</tr>
    <tr><td><strong>Reliability</strong></td><td>Auditable, comparable across companies</td><td>Definition varies — each company picks its own</td></tr>
    <tr><td><strong>Required by</strong></td><td>ASC 606 (since 2018) for all public companies with multi-year contracts</td><td>Voluntary disclosure</td></tr>
    <tr><td><strong>Where to find it</strong></td><td>10-Q or 10-K, under "Remaining Performance Obligations" in the revenue footnote</td><td>Earnings press release or investor presentation</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<p>One way to frame it: ARR is what management told you. cRPO is what the auditor signed off on. The gap between those two figures is the diligence opportunity.</p>

<h2>Why does cRPO matter for SaaS diligence?</h2>

<p>cRPO is a leading indicator the P&L can't show. Reported revenue is a backward-looking number — the recognition of contracts signed in prior periods. cRPO is the size of the next 12 months of contracted revenue. That makes the comparison between cRPO growth and reported revenue growth a directional read on the forward book:</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>cRPO growth > revenue growth.</strong> The forward book is compounding faster than recognition. Bullish.</li>
  <li><strong>cRPO growth < revenue growth.</strong> The book is shrinking relative to recognition. Bearish.</li>
  <li><strong>cRPO growth ≈ revenue growth.</strong> Steady-state.</li>
</ul>

<p>This works across companies and across quarters because cRPO is auditable. ARR is not always comparable — one company's ARR includes professional services revenue, another's includes one-time fees, a third treats multi-year deals on a duration-weighted basis. cRPO has one definition: the next 12 months of contracted revenue. Whatever management's ARR convention, the auditor reviews and signs off on cRPO.</p>

<h2>Workday Q1 FY27: the case study that triggered this piece</h2>

<p>On May 21, 2026, <a href="https://investor.workday.com/news-and-events/press-releases/news-details/2026/Workday-Announces-Fiscal-2027-First-Quarter-Financial-Results/default.aspx" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Workday reported Q1 FY27 results</a> that illustrate the value of cRPO better than any explainer can. Workday doesn't disclose ARR — it never has. The substitute it gives the market is cRPO and total RPO, and the spread between the two carried the story of the quarter.</p>

<p>The headline numbers from the press release:</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>cRPO: $8.806B, up 15.5% YoY.</strong> The 12-month forward subscription backlog.</li>
  <li><strong>Total RPO: $27.294B, up 10.9% YoY.</strong> All-years subscription backlog.</li>
  <li><strong>Total revenue: $2.542B, up 13.5% YoY.</strong> Subscription revenue $2.354B, up 14.3%.</li>
</ul>

<p>Two reads jump out. First, cRPO grew 15.5% while reported revenue grew 13.5% — a 200 bp gap that says the forward book is compounding faster than the P&L can show. Bullish signal, and it's why the stock traded up 10.8% the next session.</p>

<p>Second, the cRPO-RPO spread. cRPO grew 460 bps faster than total RPO. CFO Zane Rowe addressed this directly on the call: <em>"the difference reflected customer mix versus new offerings, noting renewal contracts typically carry shorter durations than new business"</em> (<a href="https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/05/21/workday-wday-q1-2027-earnings-call-transcript/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Workday Q1 FY27 earnings call, via The Motley Fool</a>). Translation: customers are signing two-year renewals where they used to sign three-year deals. Near-term volume is healthy, but the further-out book is growing more slowly because contract tenors have shortened.</p>

<p>You would not see any of this in the income statement. The trailing P&L showed strong revenue growth and a non-GAAP operating margin of 31.8%. The cRPO-RPO spread is where the duration shift surfaces.</p>

<h2>What is the cRPO-RPO spread?</h2>

<p>When a company discloses both cRPO and total RPO, the spread between their growth rates is a duration signal:</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>cRPO growth > total RPO growth.</strong> Contract durations are shortening. Customers are committing to fewer years even if near-term volume holds. Watch for: pricing power softening, customer caution, or renewal-mix shifts (Workday Q1 FY27: cRPO +15.5%, RPO +10.9%, 460 bp spread).</li>
  <li><strong>cRPO growth < total RPO growth.</strong> Contract durations are extending. Customers are committing further out, which signals confidence in the platform and the relationship. The strongest read possible from this metric pair.</li>
  <li><strong>Roughly equal.</strong> Duration is stable. The book is growing uniformly across years.</li>
</ul>

<p>The Workday read is "shorter contracts on roughly the same near-term volume." That's a worse read than 1Q's revenue and margin numbers suggest in isolation, but a better read than total-RPO growth alone would imply. The two figures together tell the story.</p>

<h2>Which public SaaS companies should you watch cRPO on?</h2>

<p>Every public SaaS company with multi-year subscription contracts discloses cRPO under ASC 606. The metric matters most at the ones whose contract durations and renewal mix actually move:</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Workday (WDAY).</strong> No ARR disclosure. cRPO is the only auditable forward-look.</li>
  <li><strong>ServiceNow (NOW).</strong> No ARR disclosure. Same situation as Workday.</li>
  <li><strong>Atlassian (TEAM).</strong> No ARR disclosure. cRPO is the forward-book read.</li>
  <li><strong>Salesforce (CRM).</strong> Discloses both. cRPO is the cleaner read because of how Salesforce defines ARR.</li>
  <li><strong>Snowflake (SNOW).</strong> Discloses both. cRPO + revenue growth combined gives a tighter read than RPO alone given consumption-model volatility.</li>
  <li><strong>Datadog (DDOG).</strong> Discloses both. cRPO captures committed minimums; consumption upside shows up in revenue.</li>
  <li><strong>MongoDB (MDB).</strong> Discloses both. Same pattern as Datadog: cRPO is the floor, revenue is the ceiling.</li>
</ul>

<p>If your forward-book read is ARR-only, you are flying blind on Workday, ServiceNow, and Atlassian. That's roughly $1.5T of market cap. cRPO closes the gap.</p>

<h2>What should PE Operating Partners track quarter-to-quarter?</h2>

<p>A short diligence checklist for cRPO. Run this on every public comp and every portco that uses ASC 606:</p>

<ol>
  <li><strong>cRPO YoY growth vs reported revenue YoY growth.</strong> If cRPO is outpacing revenue, the forward book is compounding faster than the trailing P&L. If revenue is outpacing cRPO, the book is shrinking relative to recognition — investigate.</li>
  <li><strong>cRPO YoY growth vs total RPO YoY growth.</strong> Widening spread = contract durations shortening. Narrowing spread = durations extending. Calculate this in basis points and track quarter-over-quarter.</li>
  <li><strong>cRPO as a percentage of next-four-quarters subscription revenue guide.</strong> A high ratio means the next 12 months are largely already contracted — lower execution risk. A low ratio means the company is relying on new bookings to hit guide.</li>
  <li><strong>cRPO sequential growth (QoQ).</strong> Filters out the YoY mix shift. Sequential deceleration is an earlier signal than YoY deceleration.</li>
  <li><strong>The footnote language.</strong> Read the actual ASC 606 disclosure. Some companies break cRPO into "billed" and "unbilled." That split tells you about invoice timing and DSO trends. It is usually a paragraph — read it.</li>
</ol>

<h2>How does cRPO fit into M&A diligence?</h2>

<p>For buy-side teams, cRPO is the forward-book figure that survives accounting scrutiny. ARR sometimes includes one-time items, professional services revenue, or other adjustments depending on how the seller defines it. cRPO is what the auditor signed off on. When the QoE workbook is being negotiated and the seller's ARR roll-forward is under question, cRPO is the independent check.</p>

<p>For private-company CFOs who want to be acquirable (or take the company public), the implication is to run the shop on a cRPO-equivalent today, even though the disclosure is not required. The discipline of tracking forward bookings on the balance sheet, rather than the marketing definition of ARR, is the difference between a strategic premium and a discount. Acquirers know a company's ARR faster and better than the company itself. They will know your cRPO too.</p>

<h2>The Pacer AI angle</h2>

<p>ARR is what management told you. cRPO is what the auditor signed off on. For PE Operating Partners with multiple portcos, for CFOs preparing for a transaction, and for M&A diligence teams pricing risk, the cRPO disclosure is the one piece of forward-revenue truth that doesn't require you to take management's word for the definition.</p>

Our <a href="/resources/board-quality-arr-snowballs/">ARR Snowball reporting</a> shows the period-over-period movements that drive both metrics. The numbers should agree. When they don't, the gap is the diligence opportunity.</p>

</div>

  <h1>What is cRPO? The Operator’s Guide to Current Remaining Performance Obligations</h1>
  <div class="post-meta">
    <span class="author">Pacer AI</span>
    <span>May 28, 2026</span>
  </div>

<div class="post-content">
<p><strong>cRPO — current Remaining Performance Obligations</strong> is the 12-month forward-bookings figure on every public SaaS company’s balance sheet. It is the dollar value of contracted revenue that will be recognized over the next 12 months, audited under <a href="https://asc.fasb.org/topic&trid=49130388" target="_blank" rel="noopener">ASC 606</a>, and disclosed in every 10-Q and 10-K since 2018. For PE Operating Partners, CFOs, and M&A diligence teams, it is the cleanest leading indicator on SaaS performance. Cleaner than ARR, because ARR is whatever management says it is, and cRPO is what the auditor signed off on.</p>

<p>Most operators still treat ARR as the gold standard for forward revenue. That’s a problem in 2026. Contract durations have been compressing across the industry, ARR definitions vary company-to-company, and three of the largest public SaaS companies (Workday, ServiceNow, and Atlassian) don’t disclose ARR at all. If you anchor on ARR, you are flying blind on a meaningful share of the market.</p>

<h2>What is cRPO?</h2>

<p>cRPO stands for <strong>current Remaining Performance Obligations</strong>. It is the portion of total Remaining Performance Obligations (RPO) that the company expects to recognize as revenue within the next 12 months. Both metrics come from the same revenue footnote in the 10-Q and 10-K, required under <a href="https://www.fasb.org/page/PageContent?pageId=/standards/accounting-standards-codification.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">FASB ASC 606 — Revenue from Contracts with Customers</a>.</p>

<p>The mechanics are simple. When a SaaS company signs a multi-year contract, the full contract value sits on the balance sheet as a performance obligation. cRPO carves out the slice that will convert to revenue in the next four quarters. Total RPO captures everything beyond that — year two, year three, and any further-out commitments.</p>

<h2>How is cRPO different from ARR?</h2>

<p>The differences matter for diligence. ARR is a management-defined run-rate metric. cRPO is an auditable, GAAP-disclosed forward-bookings figure. They measure different things, and they are not interchangeable.</p>

  <thead>
    <tr><th></th><th>cRPO</th><th>ARR</th></tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><td><strong>Source</strong></td><td>Balance sheet (audited, GAAP)</td><td>Management-disclosed (non-GAAP)</td></tr>
    <tr><td><strong>Window</strong></td><td>Next 12 months only</td><td>Annualized run-rate at point in time</td></tr>
    <tr><td><strong>Includes</strong></td><td>Signed contracts, both billed and unbilled</td><td>Active recurring subscriptions at end of period</tr>
    <tr><td><strong>Reliability</strong></td><td>Auditable, comparable across companies</td><td>Definition varies — each company picks its own</td></tr>
    <tr><td><strong>Required by</strong></td><td>ASC 606 (since 2018) for all public companies with multi-year contracts</td><td>Voluntary disclosure</td></tr>
    <tr><td><strong>Where to find it</strong></td><td>10-Q or 10-K, under “Remaining Performance Obligations” in the revenue footnote</td><td>Earnings press release or investor presentation</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<p>One way to frame it: ARR is what management told you. cRPO is what the auditor signed off on. The gap between those two figures is the diligence opportunity.</p>

<h2>Why does cRPO matter for SaaS diligence?</h2>

<p>cRPO is a leading indicator the P&L can’t show. Reported revenue is a backward-looking number — the recognition of contracts signed in prior periods. cRPO is the size of the next 12 months of contracted revenue. That makes the comparison between cRPO growth and reported revenue growth a directional read on the forward book:</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>cRPO growth > revenue growth.</strong> The forward book is compounding faster than recognition. Bullish.</li>
  <li><strong>cRPO growth < revenue growth.</strong> The book is shrinking relative to recognition. Bearish.</li>
  <li><strong>cRPO growth ≈ revenue growth.</strong> Steady-state.</li>
</ul>

<p>This works across companies and across quarters because cRPO is auditable. ARR is not always comparable — one company’s ARR includes professional services revenue, another’s includes one-time fees, a third treats multi-year deals on a duration-weighted basis. cRPO has one definition: the next 12 months of contracted revenue. Whatever management’s ARR convention, the auditor reviews and signs off on cRPO.</p>

<h2>Workday Q1 FY27: the case study that triggered this piece</h2>

<p>On May 21, 2026, <a href="https://investor.workday.com/news-and-events/press-releases/news-details/2026/Workday-Announces-Fiscal-2027-First-Quarter-Financial-Results/default.aspx" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Workday reported Q1 FY27 results</a> that illustrate the value of cRPO better than any explainer can. Workday doesn’t disclose ARR — it never has. The substitute it gives the market is cRPO and total RPO, and the spread between the two carried the story of the quarter.</p>

<p>The headline numbers from the press release:</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>cRPO: $8.806B, up 15.5% YoY.</strong> The 12-month forward subscription backlog.</li>
  <li><strong>Total RPO: $27.294B, up 10.9% YoY.</strong> All-years subscription backlog.</li>
  <li><strong>Total revenue: $2.542B, up 13.5% YoY.</strong> Subscription revenue $2.354B, up 14.3%.</li>
</ul>

<p>Two reads jump out. First, cRPO grew 15.5% while reported revenue grew 13.5% — a 200 bp gap that says the forward book is compounding faster than the P&L can show. Bullish signal, and it’s why the stock traded up 10.8% the next session.</p>

<p>Second, the cRPO-RPO spread. cRPO grew 460 bps faster than total RPO. CFO Zane Rowe addressed this directly on the call: <em>“the difference reflected customer mix versus new offerings, noting renewal contracts typically carry shorter durations than new business”</em> (<a href="https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/05/21/workday-wday-q1-2027-earnings-call-transcript/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Workday Q1 FY27 earnings call, via The Motley Fool</a>). Translation: customers are signing two-year renewals where they used to sign three-year deals. Near-term volume is healthy, but the further-out book is growing more slowly because contract tenors have shortened.</p>

<p>You would not see any of this in the income statement. The trailing P&L showed strong revenue growth and a non-GAAP operating margin of 31.8%. The cRPO-RPO spread is where the duration shift surfaces.</p>

<h2>What is the cRPO-RPO spread?</h2>

<p>When a company discloses both cRPO and total RPO, the spread between their growth rates is a duration signal:</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>cRPO growth > total RPO growth.</strong> Contract durations are shortening. Customers are committing to fewer years even if near-term volume holds. Watch for: pricing power softening, customer caution, or renewal-mix shifts (Workday Q1 FY27: cRPO +15.5%, RPO +10.9%, 460 bp spread).</li>
  <li><strong>cRPO growth < total RPO growth.</strong> Contract durations are extending. Customers are committing further out, which signals confidence in the platform and the relationship. The strongest read possible from this metric pair.</li>
  <li><strong>Roughly equal.</strong> Duration is stable. The book is growing uniformly across years.</li>
</ul>

<p>The Workday read is “shorter contracts on roughly the same near-term volume.” That’s a worse read than 1Q’s revenue and margin numbers suggest in isolation, but a better read than total-RPO growth alone would imply. The two figures together tell the story.</p>

<h2>Which public SaaS companies should you watch cRPO on?</h2>

<p>Every public SaaS company with multi-year subscription contracts discloses cRPO under ASC 606. The metric matters most at the ones whose contract durations and renewal mix actually move:</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Workday (WDAY).</strong> No ARR disclosure. cRPO is the only auditable forward-look.</li>
  <li><strong>ServiceNow (NOW).</strong> No ARR disclosure. Same situation as Workday.</li>
  <li><strong>Atlassian (TEAM).</strong> No ARR disclosure. cRPO is the forward-book read.</li>
  <li><strong>Salesforce (CRM).</strong> Discloses both. cRPO is the cleaner read because of how Salesforce defines ARR.</li>
  <li><strong>Snowflake (SNOW).</strong> Discloses both. cRPO + revenue growth combined gives a tighter read than RPO alone given consumption-model volatility.</li>
  <li><strong>Datadog (DDOG).</strong> Discloses both. cRPO captures committed minimums; consumption upside shows up in revenue.</li>
  <li><strong>MongoDB (MDB).</strong> Discloses both. Same pattern as Datadog: cRPO is the floor, revenue is the ceiling.</li>
</ul>

<p>If your forward-book read is ARR-only, you are flying blind on Workday, ServiceNow, and Atlassian. That’s roughly $1.5T of market cap. cRPO closes the gap.</p>

<h2>What should PE Operating Partners track quarter-to-quarter?</h2>

<p>A short diligence checklist for cRPO. Run this on every public comp and every portco that uses ASC 606:</p>

<ol>
  <li><strong>cRPO YoY growth vs reported revenue YoY growth.</strong> If cRPO is outpacing revenue, the forward book is compounding faster than the trailing P&L. If revenue is outpacing cRPO, the book is shrinking relative to recognition — investigate.</li>
  <li><strong>cRPO YoY growth vs total RPO YoY growth.</strong> Widening spread = contract durations shortening. Narrowing spread = durations extending. Calculate this in basis points and track quarter-over-quarter.</li>
  <li><strong>cRPO as a percentage of next-four-quarters subscription revenue guide.</strong> A high ratio means the next 12 months are largely already contracted — lower execution risk. A low ratio means the company is relying on new bookings to hit guide.</li>
  <li><strong>cRPO sequential growth (QoQ).</strong> Filters out the YoY mix shift. Sequential deceleration is an earlier signal than YoY deceleration.</li>
  <li><strong>The footnote language.</strong> Read the actual ASC 606 disclosure. Some companies break cRPO into “billed” and “unbilled.” That split tells you about invoice timing and DSO trends. It is usually a paragraph — read it.</li>
</ol>

<h2>How does cRPO fit into M&A diligence?</h2>

<p>For buy-side teams, cRPO is the forward-book figure that survives accounting scrutiny. ARR sometimes includes one-time items, professional services revenue, or other adjustments depending on how the seller defines it. cRPO is what the auditor signed off on. When the QoE workbook is being negotiated and the seller’s ARR roll-forward is under question, cRPO is the independent check.</p>

<p>For private-company CFOs who want to be acquirable (or take the company public), the implication is to run the shop on a cRPO-equivalent today, even though the disclosure is not required. The discipline of tracking forward bookings on the balance sheet, rather than the marketing definition of ARR, is the difference between a strategic premium and a discount. Acquirers know a company’s ARR faster and better than the company itself. They will know your cRPO too.</p>

<h2>The Pacer AI angle</h2>

<p>ARR is what management told you. cRPO is what the auditor signed off on. For PE Operating Partners with multiple portcos, for CFOs preparing for a transaction, and for M&A diligence teams pricing risk, the cRPO disclosure is the one piece of forward-revenue truth that doesn’t require you to take management’s word for the definition.</p>

<p>At Pacer AI, our <a href="/resources/build-customer-data-cube-in-house-or-hire/">Customer Data Cube</a> reconciles ARR, cRPO, billings, and reported revenue into a single M&A-grade view — the same reconciliation Big-4 QoE teams produce in diligence. Our <a href="/resources/board-quality-arr-snowballs/">ARR Snowball reporting</a> shows the period-over-period movements that drive both metrics. The numbers should agree. When they don’t, the gap is the diligence opportunity.</p>
